background.definition: Ewing sarcoma is a small round blue cell cancer of children and young adults, most commonly arising in the bone. Part of a family of tumors that includes peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumors, Askin tumor of the chest wall, and classic Ewing sarcoma.

list.listitem: 250 new cases in the United States each year.
Second most common bone cancer in children and young adults, after osteosarcoma.
Cause is unknown.
Cell of origin also remains unknown.
Characteristic translocation is thought to drive growth of these tumors.
EWS/FLI translocation from t(11;22) is the most common of these translocations; less common translocations have been identified.
Translocations are thought to produce an aberrant transcription factor, leading to oncogenesis.
Pain is the most common presenting symptom. C
MRI is the standard imaging approach for primary tumor. C
Metastatic evaluation includes chest CT, bone scan, and bone marrow biopsies. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually tumor of long bones leading to spiculated or "sunburst" periosteal reaction
Permeative or "moth-eaten" appearance on plain radiograph
Usually very little associated soft tissue mass
Usually multiple smaller lesions rather than single larger lesion

list.listitem: Pain is the most common symptom, reported in 89% of patients in 1 series.
Fever present in 15% to 20% of patients at initial presentation.
Average duration of symptoms prior to diagnosis is about 4 months.

Other symptoms depend on location of tumor: neurologic symptoms with paraspinal tumors; voiding dysfunction with pelvic tumors; symptoms of bone marrow suppression with extensive bone marrow involvement.
MRI is the standard imaging approach for primary tumor.
PET/CT has good accuracy for detection of metastases.
ESR and LDH are elevated in one-third of patients at diagnosis.
Alkaline phosphatase usually is not elevated, unlike the case in osteosarcoma.
Anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia may be present with bone marrow metastatic disease. Metastatic evaluation includes chest CT, bone scan, and bone marrow biopsies.
Suspect Ewing sarcoma or other bone tumor in patients with persistent bone pain. Detailed imaging of the primary tumor is best performed with an MRI.
If tumor is suspected, use core needle or open biopsy by orthopedic oncologist. If diagnosis is confirmed, use metastatic staging with chest CT, bone scan, and bilateral bone marrow biopsies.
Treatment requires systemic chemotherapy and local control of the primary tumor with surgery and/or radiation.
Multimodal approach to therapy is recommended. C
Use of ifosfamide and etoposide added to vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide improved outcomes in RCT of patients with nonmetastatic disease. B
Interval compression of chemotherapy (cycles every 2 weeks) has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with localized disease.
Approach to local control of primary tumor remains controversial. For patients with localized Ewing Sarcoma, radiotherapy or surgery alone are options, providing clear margins can be achieved. C
Multidisciplinary team approach is required, including oncology, orthopedics, general surgery, and radiation oncology specialists.
Combination multiagent chemotherapy for approximately 12 weeks prior to local control. Additional chemotherapy after local control typically to complete a total of at least 36 weeks of chemotherapy.
North American IESS-1 study demonstrated that doxorubicin added to vincristine, actinomycin, and cyclophosphamide improved outcomes for patients with nonmetastatic tumors.

North American INT-0091 study demonstrated that ifosfamide and etoposide added to vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide improved outcomes for patients with nonmetastatic tumors (69% vs. 54% 5-year survival, NNT = 7).

Children's Oncology Group Study AEWS0031 recently showed that interval compression of chemotherapy given every 2 weeks improves outcomes for localized tumors compared with standard 3-week chemotherapy cycles.
There is recent evidence of clinical activity of IGF-1R inhibitors in patients with relapsed disease, though all such agents remain investigational.
A systematic review found uncertain evidence regarding the benefit of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to intensify chemotherapy.
Local control is usually initiated after 12 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. However, the optimal mode of local control is controversial.

Most retrospective studies indicate lower local failure rate with surgery, though analyses are subject to selection bias. For patients with localized Ewing Sarcoma, radiotherapy or surgery alone are options, providing clear margins can be achieved.
Surgery with positive margins requires postoperative radiation.
If radiation is used as the only mode of local control, involved field radiation has been shown to be as effective as whole-bone radiation.
An observational study of 51 patients with Ewing Sarcoma of the neck or head found similar 3 year event free survival rates with surgery, radiation, or both.
Role of high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell rescue (transplant) for high-risk patients is controversial and under investigation.
Patients with lung metastases appear to benefit from whole-lung radiation.
Management of patients with metastatic or recurrent tumors is not standardized, and many of these patients are referred for investigational therapies.
All patients should be managed at a center with specific expertise in the management of these tumors.
Survival rate is approximately 70% for patients with localized tumors. B
Metastatic disease is the most important adverse prognostic factor. B
Approximately 25% of patients have metastatic disease at initial presentation, including lung, bone, and bone marrow distant spread. Staging studies are based on metastatic pattern.
Survivors require ongoing followup for late effects of therapy. C
Factors associated with a lower likelihood of survival include metastasis, larger tumors (>200 ml or diameter >8 cm), less than complete histologic response, and axial tumors.

A systematic review of treated Ewings sarcoma patients demonstrated a clinically relevant risk of infertility following treatment (89% of male and 13% females) likely associated with alkylating agent therapy. Patients should be appropriately counselled and steps taken to address this if required.
